newsitem.title: INDIA: Pro-India party clinches Kashmir polls.
newsitem.headline: Pro-India party clinches Kashmir polls.

text.p: The largest pro-India party in Jammu and Kashmir state has won an absolute majority in the first state assembly elections since the outbreak of a separatist rebellion in 1990, results showed on Wednesday.
The National Conference, led by former chief minister Farooq Abdullah, had won 51 seats in the 87-member assembly by 0230 GMT, a government spokesman said.
The National Conference had a commanding lead over its rivals. Trailing far behind were the Congress party and the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), each with seven seats.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's socialist Janata Dal party had five.

Abdullah, who was chief minister when the insurgency erupted in early 1990, has promised to continue a crackdown on militants. He recently said that separatists opposed to the polls should move to neighbouring Pakistan.
India accuses Pakistan, which rules over one third of the Kashmir region, of arming guerrillas. Islamabad denies the charge.
More than 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence, according to police and hospital officials.

Abdullah, who escaped two grenade attacks during the month-long elections which ended on Monday, has demanded a greater degree of autonomy for the Himalayan state, torn by the six-year separatist revolt.

His party refused to participate in general elections held earlier this year, saying the federal government of then prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao was not committed to meeting the autonomy demands.
But after Deve Gowda assumed power in June, his centre-left United Front coalition announced it would offer "maximum autonomy" to India's only Moslem majority state.
The National Conference decided to participate in last month's local assembly polls in anticipation of an autonomy package.

However, the BJP has promised to oppose any move in the federal parliament to grant special status to Jammu and Kashmir, made up of the mostly Moslem Kashmir valley, the Hindu majority Jammu region and Buddhist Ladakh.
Under the Indian constitution, the state has nominal control over its affairs except in the realms of defence, foreign affairs and communications.
But since 1952, the state's autonomous status has been gradually eroded, and Abdullah wants to recapture some of the powers as a means of quelling the separatist movement.
